card.stem: A triple glazed timber casement window is fixed in the external wall of a dwelling house, as shown in the sketch. The external wall is a 350 mm concrete block wall with an insulated cavity. The wall is plastered on both sides. The fixed frame of the window is 150 mm × 80 mm.
card.questionText: To a scale of 1:5 draw a vertical section through the top portion of the window showing the fixed window frame and the concrete lintels. Show the typical construction details from 300 mm below to a level 400 mm above the concrete lintels. Include four typical dimensions.

rows.verbatim: Any 7 of the above details (6 marks each)
rows.contextNote: Credit the best SEVEN acceptable details at 6 marks each, capped at 42. Marked details: 15 mm external plaster; 100 mm outer leaf; 50 mm residual cavity; 100 mm insulation; 100 mm inner leaf; 15 mm internal plaster; 100 × 70 mm pre-stressed concrete lintels; the 150 × 80 mm window head; triple low-e glazing; typical dimensions.

card.stem: A dwelling house built 40 years ago, as shown in the sketch, has a 300 mm external concrete block wall with a 100 mm un-insulated cavity. The owner intends to refurbish the house to improve the thermal insulation levels of the external walls by: injecting insulation into the cavity of the external walls and fixing an internal insulation system to the external walls.
card.questionText: For each insulation system listed above, show using notes and neat freehand sketches the procedures to be followed when applying the insulation system. For each system, specify the insulation material used.

rows.verbatim: Injecting the insulation into the cavity of the external wall - Notes
rows.contextNote: A valid description 6 and the type of insulation 4. Such as: by a specialist company, 22 mm holes drilled through the outer leaf at 800 mm horizontally and 1350 mm vertically, with extra holes at cills and heads; polystyrene beads with a light glue, or cellulose, pumped in; the holes filled to match.

rows.verbatim: Injecting the insulation into the cavity of the external wall - Sketch
rows.contextNote: The quality of the sketch 6 and a valid detail 4, as in the scheme’s model sketches.

rows.verbatim: Fixing an internal insulation system to the external walls - Notes
rows.contextNote: A valid description 6 and the type of insulation 4. Such as: 50 × 50 mm treated battens at 400 mm centres with insulation between, a vapour barrier and 12 mm plasterboard with a skim coat; or insulated plasterboard on dabs with mechanical fixings. Cork, wood fibre, sheep’s wool, fibreglass, polystyrene or polyurethane.

rows.verbatim: Fixing an internal insulation system to the external walls - Sketch
rows.contextNote: The quality of the sketch 6 and a valid detail 4, as in the scheme’s model sketches.

card.stem: A dwelling house built 40 years ago, as shown in the sketch, has a 300 mm external concrete block wall with a 100 mm un-insulated cavity. The owner intends to refurbish the house to improve the thermal insulation levels of the external walls by: injecting insulation into the cavity of the external walls and fixing an internal insulation system to the external walls.
card.questionText: Discuss one advantage and one disadvantage of each system of insulation.

rows.verbatim: Advantage and disadvantage of injecting insulation into the cavity
rows.contextNote: Such as: less heat loss, quick and economical, with no disturbance inside and the block’s thermal mass kept; but the cavity is bridged, damp may cross it, the holes show and the fill may leave cold spots.

rows.verbatim: Advantage and disadvantage of fixing internal insulation system
rows.contextNote: Such as: a better U-value, no change outside and local labour can do it; but rooms lose floor area, the work is disruptive, dusty and dear, and fittings must be moved.

card.questionText: List two specific safety precautions to be observed in each of the following situations and give one reason for each safety precaution listed: fitting a precast concrete window cill at ground floor level in a house; working at height when renovating an old house.

rows.verbatim: Safety precautions to be observed when fitting a precast window cill
rows.contextNote: Two precautions 5 each and reasons 5. Such as: a clear, tidy area; help to lift, in unison; steel-capped boots and gloves; the cill rested on supports before lifting into place — so it is lifted safely and feet and hands are protected.

rows.verbatim: Safety precautions when working at height
rows.contextNote: Two precautions 5 each and reasons 5. Such as: scaffolding erected by a qualified person, with hand rails and toe boards; a ladder at 1:4, extending 1.0 m above the platform, secured on level ground — a safe platform, nothing falling on those below, no slipping.

card.questionText: Explain with the aid of notes and neat freehand sketches, any five of the following: fascia; strip foundation; thermostatic valve; window board; butt hinge; rafter; solar panel; wall tie; radon barrier.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Fascia: the horizontal member fixed to the ends of the rafters, forming the eaves with the soffit; red or white deal or uPVC; it finishes the rafter ends and carries the gutter brackets. Strip foundation: the most common concrete foundation, a reinforced strip under the wall, typically three times the wall thickness wide and 300 mm thick; the wall central and the load spread at 45°. Thermostatic valve: a radiator valve set to the room temperature, regulating the flow to control the radiator’s output; inexpensive, it cuts CO₂ and energy costs. Window board: a hardwood, softwood or uPVC board, 18–30 mm thick, fixed horizontally inside the window frame, with insulation beneath against a cold bridge and airtight taped or mastic joints. Butt hinge: a brass or mild steel hinge, 12–150 mm long, of two leaves and a pin, fitted into shallow trenches with countersunk screws; used for doors, windows and boxes. Rafter: the sloping member of the roof from the eaves to the ridge board, usually white deal, typically 200 × 50 mm, secured to the wall plate and the ridge board. Solar panel: collects solar radiation and converts it to heat; usually on a south-facing roof or a ground fixing, flat plate or evacuated tube, used with other heating; reduces CO₂. Wall tie: a polypropylene or stainless steel fitting holding the two leaves of a cavity wall together as one unit and holding the insulation; typically at 900 mm horizontally and 450 mm vertically. Radon barrier: a complete, sealed flexible membrane under the whole floor and the external walls stopping radon gas entering; installed by specialists, not damaged, and sealed round service pipes.
